content.title: About
content.content: Baby Toddler fruit, with grain is a baby food puree made from apples, pears, bananas and whole wheat grains. It is intended for children from 6 months old and is fortified with vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The combination of fruit and whole grains provides both quick and slow‑release carbohydrates.
The product undergoes heat treatment that retains most of vitamins C and A.
Whole grains help develop chewing skills in infants.
The packaging is BPA‑free and safe.
No added sugar, artificial colours or flavours are used.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 support energy metabolism and nervous system development.

items.title: Source of dietary fibre
items.content: Whole grains and fruit puree aid digestion and promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Supports bone growth
items.content: The product is fortified with calcium and vitamin D, essential for strong bone formation.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Fruits provide vitamin C and carotenoids that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Energy sustenance
items.content: A mix of simple and complex carbs offers lasting satiety and stable energy levels.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Children with gluten or wheat sensitivity may experience an allergic reaction.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Small grain particles can pose a choking risk for infants under 12 months; serve as a smooth puree.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although no added sugar is present, natural fruit sugars may affect blood glucose in children predisposed to diabetes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the puree with a baby spoon, optionally thin with breast milk or formula. If desired, mash the grains with a fork before feeding.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sealed package in a cool, dry place. After opening, consume within 3‑5 days and store in the refrigerator at +2…+4 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Cilantro (Coriandrum sativum) is an annual herb widely used as a fresh garnish in cooking. Its bright‑green leaves have a distinctive citrusy aroma and are common in Asian, Latin American, and Mediterranean dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cilantro is known as coriander when referring to its seeds, and as cilantro when referring to the leaves.
In some cuisines the herb is added at the end of cooking to preserve its fresh flavor.
A genetic variation causes a portion of the population to perceive cilantro’s taste as soapy.
The seeds are used as a spice, while the leaves are used fresh.
Cilantro can be easily grown at home in pots.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: The leaves contain vitamin C, quercetin, and other polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Essential oils and dietary fiber stimulate bile production and improve intestinal motility.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Cilantro provides vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A generous serving of cilantro adds minimal calories, making it suitable for weight‑conscious diets.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: The herb supplies potassium, magnesium, and iron, supporting heart function and blood health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cilantro, such as skin itching or swelling.

items.title: Microbial contamination
items.content: Raw leafy greens can be contaminated with bacteria (e.g., E. coli); thorough washing before use is recommended.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Cilantro may enhance the effects of anticoagulant medications, so people on such drugs should consult a healthcare professional.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use cilantro fresh in salads, salsas, soups, marinades, and as a garnish for fish, meat, and rice dishes. It can be blended into smoothies or sauces. For maximum flavor, sprinkle chopped leaves over finished dishes just before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cilantro in the refrigerator wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel inside a sealed bag. It stays fresh for 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze the leaves in ice‑cube trays with a little water.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit salad without citrus fruits is a mix of fresh berries, apples, pears, bananas and grapes, dressed with light whipped cream. The salad offers a sweet‑slightly tangy flavor and a soft texture, suitable as a dessert or a light snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The salad is commonly served in summer when fresh fruit is abundant.
Whipped cream adds airiness and makes the dish feel more festive.
Excluding citrus makes it safe for people with citrus allergies.
Combining different fruits increases the variety of vitamins and minerals in one bowl.
Traditionally the salad is garnished with mint or sprinkled with nuts for texture contrast.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Apples, pears and bananas provide B1, B2 and B6, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fruits, especially apples and pears, are high in fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Berries and grapes contain polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Calcium from cream
items.content: Whipped cream adds calcium, important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Heart‑supporting potassium
items.content: Bananas and apples provide potassium, which aids normal blood pressure.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit salad can be high in natural sugars; people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Whipped cream contains lactose, so lactose‑intolerant individuals should use dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: If the salad is garnished with nuts, be aware of possible allergic reactions.

items.title: Fruit oxidation
items.content: Some fruits (e.g., apples) may brown quickly; it is best to serve the salad soon after preparation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, optionally adding an extra dollop of whipped cream on top. It can be eaten with a spoon or used as a filling for pancakes or waffles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Add whipped cream right before serving to preserve its fluffiness.

content.title: About
content.content: Funnel cake is a deep‑fried batter dessert popular at fairs and festivals. A thin batter made of flour, eggs, milk, sugar and leavening is poured through a funnel into hot oil, creating crisp, lace‑like spirals that are dusted with powdered sugar after frying.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Although now associated with American fairs, funnel cake has roots in German and Scandinavian street food traditions.
The name comes from the way the batter is “funneled” into the oil.
In the 1930s the treat became an iconic symbol of summer carnivals in the United States.
There are many variations – topped with berries, chocolate, caramel – but the classic version is simply powdered sugar.
The batter is usually prepared fresh right before frying to keep the texture light and airy.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: The high carbohydrate content provides a rapid boost of energy, useful for active individuals.

items.title: Small amount of protein
items.content: Flour and eggs supply modest amounts of plant and animal protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The batter contains thiamine, niacin and folate, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: High sugar and fat content
items.content: The combination of sugar and deep‑fried oil makes the dessert calorie‑dense and may contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional recipes use wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Trans fats from reused oil
items.content: Reusing frying oil can generate trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, straight from the fryer, generously dusted with powdered sugar. Optional toppings include fresh berries, fruit sauces, whipped cream, or ice cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Funnel cake is best enjoyed immediately. If needed, keep it in an airtight container at room temperature for no more than 2 hours, as it loses crispness. For longer storage, freeze individual portions and reheat in the oven.

content.title: About
content.content: Hard seltzer is a carbonated alcoholic beverage made by fermenting sugar, then adding flavorings and often a modest amount of alcohol (usually 4‑5%). It is light, low‑calorie, and typically contains between 0.5% and 2% alcohol, making it a popular alternative to beer and cocktails.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hard seltzer originated in the United States in the early 2010s and quickly became a bar‑culture trend.
Unlike traditional sodas, hard seltzer often uses neutral spirit distilled from corn or rice.
Most brands offer more than 30 flavors, ranging from classic berry to exotic options like passion fruit or cucumber‑mint.
Because of its low sugar and calorie count (about 30‑50 kcal per 12 oz), hard seltzer is marketed as a “healthier” alcoholic drink.
Some variants are fortified with vitamins and electrolytes, resembling sports drinks.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Hard seltzer typically contains 30‑50 kcal per can, far fewer than beer or sugary cocktails.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: Most brands use minimal sugar or sugar substitutes, resulting in a lower glycemic impact.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The carbonated water component helps maintain fluid balance, especially when the drink is enriched with electrolytes.

items.title: No artificial colors
items.content: Many producers rely on natural flavorings and avoid artificial dyes, making the product cleaner.

items.title: Food‑pairing versatility
items.content: Its neutral taste and light fizz make it easy to pair with a wide range of dishes, from light appetizers to seafood.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Even a modest alcohol percentage can lead to intoxication if consumed in large quantities.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: The bubbles may cause discomfort for people with sensitive stomachs or IBS.

items.title: Sugar substitutes
items.content: Some versions contain artificial sweeteners that can trigger individual reactions.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Flavorings may contain traces of nuts, dairy, or gluten.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Alcohol, even in small amounts, can amplify the effects of certain medications.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Hard seltzer is usually served chilled, straight from the can or poured over ice. It can be enjoyed on its own, used in cocktails as a substitute for champagne, or mixed with fruit juices and fresh herbs for light, refreshing drinks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store hard seltzer in a cool, dark place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep it refrigerated and consume within 2‑3 days to maintain freshness and carbonation.

hot-dog-sandwich-turkey-on-wheat-bun.title: Hot dog sandwich, turkey, on wheat bun

content.title: About
content.content: A hot dog sandwich with turkey on a wheat bun is a handheld meal featuring a grilled or baked turkey patty placed inside a soft wheat bun, typically topped with mustard, ketchup, pickles, and onions. The nutritional profile combines turkey protein, wheat carbohydrates, and a modest amount of fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is considered a leaner meat compared with beef, making it a popular choice for healthier diets.
A wheat bun provides complex carbs that release energy more slowly than refined flour breads.
The classic hot dog originated in the United States in the early 1900s; turkey versions appeared later as a lower‑fat alternative.
The sandwich is often served with vegetable toppings, boosting vitamin and fiber content.
Turkey is rich in tryptophan, an amino acid involved in serotonin production.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Turkey provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, turkey contains less saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains selenium
items.content: Selenium from turkey contributes to antioxidant protection of cells.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index
items.content: A wheat bun has a moderate GI, helping maintain stable blood sugar when eaten in reasonable portions.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to bird meat, including turkey.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared hot dogs often contain added salt and preservatives, so total sodium intake should be monitored.

items.title: Gluten in the bun
items.content: Wheat buns contain gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich can be calorie‑dense due to sauces and the bun; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is convenient to eat with your hands, but you can split it and add fresh lettuce, tomato, or avocado for extra nutrients. For a lighter taste, use mustard or a yogurt‑based sauce instead of sweet ketchup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled hot dog in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for up to 2 days. Keep the bun in a dry place or sealed bag to prevent drying out. Turkey can be frozen for up to 3 months, and the bun for up to 1 month.

content.title: About
content.content: Lasagna with chicken or turkey is a baked casserole made of pasta sheets, béchamel sauce, tomato sauce, cheese, and tender poultry meat. The dish combines aromatic herbs, creamy texture, and the protein benefits of bird meat, making it a popular choice for family meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Italian lasagna is made with beef, but chicken and turkey versions have become popular in the US and Europe for their lighter flavor.
Chicken and turkey retain most of their nutrients during baking when not overcooked.
A layer of béchamel in classic lasagna helps retain moisture, giving the dish a silky mouthfeel.
Some regions use whole‑grain pasta to increase fiber content.
Lasagna can be prepared ahead of time and reheated, making it convenient for meal planning.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Lower fat compared to beef
items.content: Poultry contains less saturated fat, making the dish more heart‑friendly.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry is high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium from cheese and béchamel
items.content: Cheese and dairy‑based sauce supply calcium important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Fiber from pasta and vegetables
items.content: Using whole‑grain pasta and adding vegetables boosts dietary fiber.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese and béchamel may trigger reactions in people sensitive to milk.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce and processed cheese can be high in salt; those with hypertension should watch portions.

items.title: Undercooked poultry
items.content: Insufficiently cooked chicken or turkey can harbor harmful bacteria; ensure internal temperature reaches 165 °F (74 °C).

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Layers of cheese and sauce add calories; proper portion control helps avoid overeating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil lasagna sheets until al dente, sauté chicken or turkey with onion and herbs, prepare tomato and béchamel sauces. In a baking dish layer pasta, sauce, meat, cheese, and repeat. Bake at 350 °F (180 °C) for 30‑40 minutes until golden. Serve hot, garnished with fresh basil or parsley.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftover lasagna to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Reheat until the interior reaches 165 °F (74 °C).

potato-french-fries-with-chili-and-chees.title: Potato French Fries with Chili and Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: Potato French fries with chili and cheese are fried potato sticks topped with a spicy chili blend and melted cheese. The dish combines the crisp texture of fries, the heat of chili, and the creamy flavor of cheese, making it a popular snack and side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: French fries first appeared in the United States in the early 1900s and quickly became a street food staple.
The chili‑cheese combination originates from Mexican cuisine, where hot sauces are often paired with melted cheese.
There are many cheese options, from mild cheddar to spicy pepper‑jack.
Chili contains capsaicin, which can boost metabolism.
Fries are commonly served in cardboard containers that are easy to recycle.

items.title: Potassium source
items.content: Potatoes are rich in potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, an antioxidant that strengthens the immune system.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Carbohydrates in potatoes provide quick energy, useful during active periods.

items.title: Capsaicin in chili
items.content: Capsaicin may help accelerate metabolism and relieve minor pain.

items.title: Calcium and phosphorus from cheese
items.content: Cheese adds calcium and phosphorus, essential for bone health.

items.title: High fat and calorie content
items.content: Fried potatoes and cheese make the dish calorie‑dense; moderation is important.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Salt used in frying and seasoning can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: Spicy food sensitivity
items.content: Chili can irritate the stomach and esophagus in individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Trans fats from improper frying
items.content: Reusing oil can create trans fats, which are harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot, sprinkling extra cheese and fresh chili to taste. Add sour cream, guacamole, or ketchup if desired. Pairs well with beer or soft drinks.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours and reheat in the oven, not the microwave, to retain crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Prunes are dried plums of special varieties (Prunus domestica) that are high in sugar and can be dried with the pit without fermenting. Prunes have dark, sticky, soft flesh with a sweet-tart flavor. They are eaten as a snack and added to desserts, baked goods, porridge, sauces, and meat dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Special plum varieties with a high sugar content are used for prunes.
In the United States, prunes have been allowed to be called dried plums since 2000.
One of the best-known production regions is Agen in France.
Prunes have long been paired with meat, such as chicken, duck, and beef, in Russian and European cooking.
Plums used for prunes are usually smaller and more oval than table varieties.

items.title: Contain fiber and sorbitol
items.content: These compounds help keep bowel movements regular.

items.title: Contain potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Contain vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K plays a role in blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contain polyphenols
items.content: The phenolic compounds in prunes have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Studied for bone health
items.content: Prunes are being studied in relation to maintaining bone density, but evidence is still limited.

items.title: Diarrhea and bloating
items.content: Because of fiber and sorbitol, a large amount of prunes can cause diarrhea, gas, and cramps.

items.title: Sugar and calories
items.content: Prunes are high in calories and sugar, so portions should be moderate.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: People with kidney disease who need to limit potassium should consult a doctor.

items.title: Sulfites and pits
items.content: Some prunes are treated with sulfites, and fruit sold with pits may contain a pit that can damage teeth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Prunes can be eaten as a snack or added to porridge, yogurt, baked goods, desserts, sauces, and meat or poultry dishes. To soften hard prunes, soak them in warm water for a while. A small handful is enough.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prunes in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place; they keep longer in the refrigerator. Discard fruit that is moldy, smells sour, or shows signs of fermentation.
